## Headline: the team's belief is confirmed, and the overlap is larger than they think

The Sharjah Tourism Innovation Hackathon 2025 (1 to 2 November 2025, AUS Main Building, run by SCTDA with the AUS Department of Computer Science and Engineering) was won by team Hayyakum from AUS with "Sharjah Quest" (https://www.aus.edu/media/news/sharjah-tourism-innovation-hackathon-at-aus-reimagines-travel-and-tourism-experience). The AUS release describes it as a gamified tourism application in which visitors collect digital stamps, unlock mascots, and follow curated itineraries to local sites and businesses. Team member Mahmoud Darwish called it an "augmented reality-powered mobile adventure that turns the city into an interactive game," with quests, stamps, badges, and leaderboards across museums, souqs, heritage houses, natural sites, and local SMEs; the team framed it around spreading footfall to neighborhood businesses, UAE Vision 2031, and inclusivity (same AUS URL). Sharjah24 and the pre-event coverage independently call it an augmented reality app with interactive digital passports and heritage-based challenges (https://sharjah24.ae/en/Articles/2025/11/06/Innovation-Hackathon-reimagines-tourism-experience-at-AUS; https://www.onearabia.me/business/innovation-hackathon-reimagines-tourism-experience-at-aus-011-129847.html). The prize was AED 20,000 and a presentation at SITTF 2025.

In practice, this means the 2025 winner already combined AR, curated route guidance, and gamification. The team's draft therefore overlaps with Sharjah Quest on three features (AR guide, route planning, and the treasure-hunt or badge layer), not only on the gamification feature they planned to replace.

## The 2025 winners are on the 2026 mentor list

The AUS release names the Hayyakum members as Mahmoud Darwish, Amr Mohi Aldeen, Mohamad Dabbagh, and Afif Zughayer (https://www.aus.edu/media/news/sharjah-tourism-innovation-hackathon-at-aus-reimagines-travel-and-tourism-experience). The 2026 mentor roster supplied by the organizers lists "Mahmoud Darwish (Founder, ReteIntel)" and "Afif Zughayer (Founder, Amana Vision)." The names match exactly. A LinkedIn search snippet for Darwish's profile (https://www.linkedin.com/in/darwish-mahmoud/) describes him as an AUS computer engineering student who presented Sharjah Quest on the SITTF 2025 main stage. I could not fetch LinkedIn directly (HTTP 999), and neither "ReteIntel" nor "Amana Vision" is indexed in web search, so the company affiliations are unverified; the identity match rests on the exact names in an AUS-run event one year later. The practical consequence is that two mentors circulating in the room today built the AR gamified guide the team's draft resembles.

## Full 2025 podium

- First, AED 20,000: Hayyakum (AUS), Sharjah Quest, as above.
- Second, AED 15,000: Nomad (AUS; Rana Gharaibeh, Halla Daas, Osama Ali, Moustafa Mughrabi), a coral reef health monitoring system that uses underwater vibrations to help Sharjah protect and showcase its marine life (https://sharjah24.ae/en/Articles/2025/11/06/Innovation-Hackathon-reimagines-tourism-experience-at-AUS).
- Third, AED 10,000: trail/s (Ajman University; Jon Zaccary Regala, Nouran Talal, Samia Bayoumi, Maryam Al Shanqiti), a unified accessibility platform for people of determination that recommends accessible places, acts as a virtual tour guide, and lets tourists rent assistive devices such as smart wheelchairs; Ajman describes it as a website with a planned browser extension (https://www.ajman.ac.ae/en/news/2025/ajman-university-students-win-third-place-at-sharjah-tourism-innovation-hackathon-2025).

Note that second and third place were sustainability and inclusion plays with a narrow, concrete mechanism, not broad platforms.

## Other finalists: only partial, self-reported evidence

No official source publishes finalists beyond the top three. Scale figures: about 500 applicants from 29 universities, 80 students from 11 universities shortlisted (https://sharjah24.ae/en/Articles/2025/11/06/Innovation-Hackathon-reimagines-tourism-experience-at-AUS); Ajman University counts this as 20 teams (Ajman URL above). LinkedIn search snippets show a team of Bashaar Naik, Abdulrahman Khalifa, Ehsan Fijhas, and Samir Daadouch claiming a "Most Innovative Hack" award for a tech-embedded tourist destination with a prototype hologram experience (https://ae.linkedin.com/in/bashaar-naik; https://www.linkedin.com/in/abdulrahman-khalifa-402693336/). This award appears in no official release, so treat it as unconfirmed.

## 2025 theme and judging criteria, and the 2026 weights

The 2025 theme was smart, sustainable tourism; the pre-event announcement phrased it as "Innovative & Sustainable Solutions in Technology for the Future of Tourism" (https://www.travelandtourworld.com/news/article/sharjah-invites-young-innovators-to-transform-tourism-with-new-hackathon-heres-all-you-need-to-know/). The 2025 panel judged clarity of the problem, relevance to Sharjah and the theme, practicality and scalability, potential value creation, innovative use of technology, and overall quality of presentation (Sharjah24 URL above). The 2025 judges and mentors were never named publicly.

The official AUS CSE page for the 2026 edition publishes weighted criteria: startup viability and commercial feasibility 20%, potential impact and value creation 20%, innovative utilization of emerging technologies 20%, problem definition clarity 10%, relevance to the theme 10%, relevance to Sharjah and the UAE context 10%, creativity and quality of presentation 10% (https://auscse.com/hackathon/). The same page confirms 10 shortlisted teams pitch for 5 minutes, accepted formats include concept pitch, MVP, data visualizations, 1 to 3 minute video, or UX/UI prototypes, and all ideas must be developed during the hackathon. Commercial feasibility, absent from the 2025 list, is now worth as much as the technology.

## Edition history and SITTF stage

2025 was the first edition: Sharjah24 lists the hackathon as a new category of the 12th SITTF (https://sharjah24.ae/en/Articles/2025/11/19/Sharjah-Tourism-Forum-launches-its-12th-edition), and the SITTF 2025 agenda carries an 11:15 to 11:25 slot titled "SITTF-Sharjah Tourism Innovation Hackathon Winner Presentation" (https://shf.sharjahtourism.ae/media/fkbnw1ez/agenda-v12-sittf.pdf). On 8 April 2026 SCTDA and AUS signed an MoU making the hackathon an annual, co-designed event (https://sharjah24.ae/en/Articles/2026/04/09/Ma03; https://gulfnews.com/uae/how-sharjahs-new-university-partnership-will-drive-tourism-opportunities-in-the-uae-1.500501107).

## What could not be found

No Gulf News, Khaleej Times, or The National coverage of the 2025 results exists in search (Gulf News covered only the 2026 MoU). No Instagram posts surfaced. The WAM article exists (https://www.wam.ae/en/article/bmkxm3s-innovation-hackathon-reimagines-tourism-experience) but its body could not be fetched. No Sheraa page mentions the hackathon. No full finalist list, no 2025 judge or mentor names, and no 2025 archived version of the event page were retrievable.

## Official destination apps

**Sharjah (SCTDA).** The only SCTDA app on the App Store is Shj AI Guide: a voice and text chatbot in English, Arabic, German, Russian, and Chinese for planning, booking, and discovering attractions. Its last update was version 7.0 on 21 December 2022; it has no AR, no map, no itinerary builder, no sustainability content, and too few ratings to display (https://apps.apple.com/us/app/shj-ai-guide/id1480995300). SharjahVerse (October 2022, Multiverse Labs) is a headset metaverse of selected attractions, not a visitor-side mobile tool (https://www.ttgasia.com/2022/10/12/sharjah-establishes-in-metaverse/). visitsharjah.com has static suggested itineraries and no app links, chatbot, or interactive map (https://www.visitsharjah.com/). Sharjah Museums Authority's VGuide SMA (April 2025) is an audio guide with sign-language support and no AR (https://apps.apple.com/us/app/vguide-sma/id6740347232). The Sharjah Archaeology Authority Metaverse Centre (December 2024) simulates a Mleiha excavation but needs a Meta Quest (https://www.wam.ae/en/article/b6qkbwj-saa-launches-global-digital-platform-for-cultural).

**Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Saudi.** Visit Dubai (version 11.2.1) offers AI-powered recommendations, custom itineraries, booking, and offline access; no AR, no sustainability (https://apps.apple.com/us/app/visit-dubai-travel-guide/id925400191). Visit Abu Dhabi lists eight languages, Near Me, an interactive map, and Tripadvisor reviews; no AI, AR, or itinerary builder (https://visitabudhabi.ae/en/plan-your-trip/visit-abu-dhabi-mobile-app). Visit Saudi's SARA is a beta conversational guide unveiled at WTM London in November 2024 (https://www.arabnews.com/node/2578602/saudi-arabia). Nusuk has over 130 services, a voice and text Nusuk AI assistant, and real-time crowd density with shortest routes; it is the only Gulf official app that surfaces crowd data, and it does so for pilgrim safety, not sustainability (https://gulfnews.com/world/gulf/saudi/saudi-arabia-nusuk-app-unveils-new-features-to-enhance-pilgrim-experience-in-mecca-and-medina-1.500039691).

## AR and historical reconstruction

- AthAR+ (Atharcom FZC, version 1.0 on 6 November 2025) is a UAE-wide iPhone app with 3D reconstructions of monuments, AR navigation, point-collecting challenges, and English/Arabic; it names no sites, has no AI, and no ratings (https://apps.apple.com/py/app/athar/id6754697595). This is the closest direct overlap with the team's AR feature list.
- Sharjah Fort (Al Hisn) AR, built by AUS students under Dr. Suhail Dahdal and shown at WTM November 2023, uses gesture recognition and AI-animated historical figures on site (https://www.aus.edu/node/102406). Khor Fakkan Resistance Monument AR (SMA and Sheraa) uses area-target tracking, on site only (https://gulfnews.com/amp/uae/government/sharjah-museums-authority-brings-khor-fakkans-resistance-monument-to-life-1.94466380).
- Louvre Abu Dhabi's "A Journey Through History" (August 2025) is a 25-minute, ten-person wireless VR installation by Small Creative, running 12 months (https://gulfnews.com/uae/people/louvre-abu-dhabi-unveils-vr-time-travel-experience-a-journey-through-history-1.500229280). Expo City Dubai's app handles tickets, GPS map, and Smart Queue; its Snapchat AR cube closed 31 March 2022 (https://campaignme.com/snapchat-and-expo-2020-dubai-invite-visitors-to-explore-the-power-of-connections-across-the-physical-and-digital-worlds/).
- HistoPad (Histovery) is a rented AR tablet at 18 European sites, shown at the Expo 2020 France pavilion (https://www.khaleejtimes.com/lifestyle/expo-2020-dubai-how-france-used-ar-technology-to-bring-notre-dame-de-paris-to-life). Lithodomos sold 360-degree VR reconstructions of 22 ancient sites; no 2024-2026 coverage found (https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1673/). Timelooper's location-locked Cardboard VR app is gone from its site, which now sells museum exhibit services (https://www.timelooper.com/). Hidden Florence is a free GPS-triggered audio walk over a 1584 map with character narrators, no AR (https://news-archive.exeter.ac.uk/2014/august/title_406169_en.html).

## AI trip planners, 2024-2026

Google AI Mode Canvas (18 November 2025) builds a side-panel itinerary with live flight and hotel prices and Maps reviews; booking is not live (https://www.techloy.com/googles-ai-mode-can-now-plan-your-entire-trip/). Gemini Live's free camera mode already answers "what is this building" with history and hours (https://true-tech.net/gemini-live-with-camera-and-screen-sharing-unveiled/), so generic landmark recognition is no longer a differentiator. Mindtrip (11 million POIs, free, editable itineraries), Layla (Skyscanner and Booking, offline, USD 49 per year), and GuideGeek (WhatsApp; a tester got identical itineraries for EUR 900 and EUR 2,000 budgets) are reviewed at https://www.unite.ai/best-ai-tools-for-travel-planning/ and https://t3n.de/news/?p=1622515. Tripadvisor Trips (July 2023, OpenAI) produces day-by-day plans without conversation (https://tripadvisor.mediaroom.com/Tripadvisor-launches-AI-powered-travel-planning-product). UAE entrants: Obaid claims a Ministry of Tourism partnership (https://apps.apple.com/us/app/-/id6755113763); DubAI runs at chat.dubai.ae (https://scoopempire.com/move-over-chatgpt-dubai-introduces-its-own-ai-dubai/). None expose crowd, carbon, or season data.

## UAE academic and hackathon work

Last year's winner, Sharjah Quest by Team Hayyakum (AED 20,000), was an AR digital passport with stamps, mascots, badges, leaderboards, and curated itineraries; the team already claimed its guidance "spreads visitor traffic" (https://www.aus.edu/node/121001). Two of its four members, Mahmoud Darwish and Afif Zughayer, share names with two of this year's mentors; verify in person. Second was Nomad (coral reef monitoring), third TRAIL/S (accessibility, Ajman University); 20 teams competed and criteria included relevance to Sharjah, practicality, and value creation (https://www.ajman.ac.ae/en/news/2025/ajman-university-students-win-third-place-at-sharjah-tourism-innovation-hackathon-2025). An Amity Dubai IEEE paper (December 2025) tested Unity and Vuforia AR with QR triggers at three UAE heritage sites and reported 25 to 30% higher engagement (https://dir.muni.ac.ug/items/966c46da-6fb5-4679-b5b2-4b504ffad165/full). Zayed University published a VR cultural-tourism study at WMSCI 2025 (https://zuscholars.zu.ac.ae/works/7713). No public release of Sharjah Quest was found.

## Sustainability precedents outside the region

ESA's Rural Tourism 5.0 ran an "attract and disperse" eco-algorithm in Cornwall and the Lake District in 2024: visitors rose 13.31%, car use fell 7.13%, cycling rose 23% (https://business.esa.int/projects/rt50). A 2024 TU Munich study found sustainability labels and crowd-season indicators significantly shift user choices (https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.11243). Dubai's Sustainable Tourism Stamp covers 237 hotels with no visitor-facing app (https://www.khaleejtimes.com/business/including-atlantis-the-palm-conrad-237-dubai-hotels-win-sustainability-stamp). Sharjah's nature-based stays grew 5% in August 2026 (https://www.khaleejtimes.com/sharjah-nature-based-resort-stays-5-rise-in-guests-august-2026-vs-2025-ecotourism-shurooq).

## Defensible differentiation (150 words)

Every official Gulf app answers "what is here"; none answers "when and how should I visit so the place survives". Sharjah has the assets: Kalba's Ramsar mangroves, Al Hefaiyah, Mleiha, the Heart of Sharjah souqs, and 2022-era digital tools that no longer compete. The defensible position is a web-first guide whose AI plans each stop against three live signals: crowd level, heat and season, and transport carbon. The itinerary shows a sustainability score per plan, nudges visitors toward off-peak windows and lower-impact routes, and moves spend from four crowded sites toward Shurooq's east-coast and desert sites. AR is the delivery layer, not the pitch: a browser AR view of a souq or fort at an earlier period, with the AI narrator explaining what is fragile about it today. Anonymized flow data returns to SCTDA as a dispersal dashboard. Sharjah Quest gamified visits; AthAR+ reconstructs monuments; this plans for preservation.

## (a) SCTDA strategy, sustainability, digital products

SCTDA's September 2024 "Connected Meeting" strategy lists public-private partnership, Sharjah Airport expansion, year-round events, new destinations and marine transport, service quality, and "strategic use of AI solutions"; no numeric target was published (https://www.sharjahtourism.ae/news/sharjah-welcomes-1-057-million-hotel-guests-in-8-months-and-unveils-strategy-to-further-boost-the-tourism-sector/). At GITEX October 2024 SCTDA launched a "Sustainable Tourism AI Assistant" in 40+ languages that advises on energy, waste, and sustainable mobility, crowdsources vetted solutions, and aligns with UN Tourism's sustainability statistical framework (https://www.sharjahtourism.ae/news/sctda-unveils-sustainable-tourism-ai-assistant-in-40-languages-to-drive-sustainability-in-the-sector/). At ATM April 2025 SCTDA launched the "Visit Sharjah" brand and a four-pillar strategy: promotion, industry and facilities development, regulation and star ratings, and CSR plus community-based tourism; Al Midfa called "innovation and sustainability" the two pillars of growth (https://gulfnews.com/business/exceptional-authentic-journey-sharjah-unveils-new-tourism-vision-to-attract-visitors-with-unique-offerings-1.500111412). In April 2026 SCTDA signed an MoU with AUS at House of Wisdom, citing the 2025 hackathon as the trigger (https://sharjah24.ae/en/Articles/2026/04/09/Ma14). Earlier SCTDA digital products: 2019 "Fatima" chatbot in Arabic, English, German, Chinese, and Russian (https://labiba.ai/sa/en/news/27); 2022 SharjahVerse metaverse and "Shj AI Guide" robot (https://www.zawya.com/en/press-release/events-and-conferences/scdta-launches-sharjahverse-and-shj-ai-guide-robot-at-gitex-global-2022-jhvzdfhn). No current consumer "Visit Sharjah" app and no numeric SCTDA sustainability or 2030 visitor target were found. Shurooq (a separate authority) runs the eco side: Sharjah Collection, Dh300 million, seven retreats, 154 units, including Nomad Kalba with 20 solar cabins (https://gulfnews.com/business/tourism/for-sharjah-slow-travel-boom-pays-off-new-eco-retreat-to-launch-in-q4-25-1.500237737); Mleiha National Park, 34.2 km², Emiri Decree 16 of 2024 (https://www.wam.ae/en/article/bluqjmk-mleiha-national-park-showcases-210000-years-uae). EPAA showcased 13 reserves at the IUCN Congress, October 2025 (https://www.wam.ae/en/article/bm4uwlg-epaa-participates-iucn-world-conservation-congress).

## (b) Visitor statistics

2024 (SCTDA, 30 April 2025): about 1.6 million hotel guests, +11%; Russia 270,000+ (+18%), India 170,000+ (+6%), Europe 100,000+ (+16%), China 60,000+ (+828%); Arab share: Oman 6%, Saudi Arabia 5%, Egypt 4%, Syria 3%, Iraq 3% (https://www.sharjahtourism.ae/news/sharjah-welcomed-1-6-million-hotel-guests-in-2024-reflecting-an-11-increase/). January to August 2024: 1.057 million, occupancy 66%, Russia 21%, UAE domestic 11%, India 10%, Oman 6% (same SCTDA strategy URL above). Q1 2025: 486,000 guests (Gulf News URL above). India, January to July 2025: about 130,000, +38% (https://sharjah24.ae/en/Articles/2025/09/08/Sharjah-Tourism-Authority-wraps-up-successful-2025-India-Roadshow). Full-year 2025 (Cavendish Maxwell, June 2026): 2.1 million guests (+22%), revenue Dh780 million (+20%), occupancy 78%, ADR Dh305, average stay two nights, 102 hotels, 10,700 keys (https://gulfnews.com/business/tourism/sharjah-hotels-draw-21-million-guests-as-airport-traffic-fuels-tourism-boom-1.500576026). Forbes Middle East 2026 attributes "over 2 million, +22%, 102 hotels, $212.4 million" to SCTDA (https://www.forbesmiddleeast.com/lists/?p=88423). No SCTDA release with a 2025 source-market split was found; note that +22% to 2.1 million implies a 1.72 million base, not 1.6 million. Sharjah Airport 2025: 19.48 million passengers, +13.9% from 17.1 million (https://www.wam.ae/en/article/byc8spi-sharjah-airport-welcomes-more-than-194-million).

## (c) Key sites

Heritage: Heart of Sharjah, 35,000 m², five phases, 2025 target, on the UNESCO tentative list (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_of_Sharjah). Al Hisn Fort built 1823, demolished 1969, reopened as a 12-gallery museum on 22 April 2015 (https://www.khaleejtimes.com/uae/restored-al-hisn-sharjah-fort-opens-to-public-as-a-museum). Souq Al Arsah about 200 years old (https://www.thenationalnews.com/uae/old-sharjah-souq-a-look-into-yesteryear-1.426782). Bait Al Naboodah, c. 1845, pearl merchant Obaid bin Isa Al Shamsi, reopened 2018 (https://www.wam.ae/en/article/hszr6xmm-bait-naboodah-opens-after-major-restoration-work).

Culture: Museum of Islamic Civilization opened June 2008, 5,000+ artefacts (https://www.khaleejtimes.com/article/more-than-5000-artefacts-on-display-at-islamic-museum). Sharjah Art Foundation founded 2009; Biennial 16 ran 6 February to 15 June 2025 (https://www.sharjahart.org/en/press/details/sharjah-art-foundation-announces-the-dates-for-march-meeting-2025-and-more-details-on-sharjah-biennial-16-events-and-programmes). Rain Room, first permanent edition, opened 29 April 2018 in Al Majarrah (https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2018/05/01/its-not-about-rain-its-about-robots-first-permanent-rain-room-opens-in-the-uae). House of Wisdom opened 9 December 2020, Foster + Partners, 305,000 books, 200,000 digital (https://gulfnews.com/amp/story/uae%2Fsharjah-ruler-opens-unique-futuristic-library---house-of-wisdom-1.75770673).

Nature: Mleiha Archaeological Centre opened January 2016 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mleiha_Archaeological_Centre). Faya Palaeolandscape inscribed UNESCO World Heritage 11 July 2025, first desert Palaeolithic site, 200,000+ years, management plan 2024 to 2030 (https://www.khaleejtimes.com/uae/sharjah-faya-unesco-world-heritage-list). Buhais Geology Park opened January 2020, Hopkins Architects (https://www.dezeen.com/2020/01/22/buhais-geology-park-interpretive-centre-hopkins-architects-sharjaha/amp/). Al Hefaiyah opened 2016, 12 km², Arabian leopard (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Hefaiyah_Conservation_Centre). Khor Kalba Mangrove Centre opened April 2021 (https://www.khaleejtimes.com/uae/kalba-gets-another-mangrove-sanctuary); joined Wetlands Link International February 2025 (https://www.wam.ae/en/article/bi9jh78-khor-kalba-mangrove-centre-joins-wetlands-link). Wasit Wetland Centre won the 2019 Aga Khan Award (https://gulftoday.ae/News/2019/09/15/Wasit-Wetland-Centre-wins-Aga-Khan-Architecture-Award). Khorfakkan Amphitheatre opened 14 December 2020, 3,600 seats (https://gulftoday.ae/Culture/2020/12/20/Thousands-visit-newly-opened-Khorfakkan--Amphitheatre-in-Sharjah-to-watch-heroic-film). Al Noor Island opened December 2015, 45,470 m², TripAdvisor top-10 Middle East 2024 (https://gulftoday.ae/business/2024/07/11/al-noor-island-listed-among-top-10-attractions-in-the-middle-east).

Leisure: Al Qasba opened 2005 with the Eye of the Emirates, since moved to Al Montazah (https://blooloop.com/theme-park/news/eye-emirates-wheel/). Al Majaz Waterfront launched 28 March 2010 (https://sharjah24.ae/en/Articles/2024/08/14/NJ268). Sharjah Safari opened February 2022, Dh1 billion (https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20220222005670/en/).

## (d) Events

Sharjah Light Festival, 15th edition, 3 to 15 February 2026, 13 sites, Light Village with 75+ national projects (https://sharjah24.ae/en/Articles/2026/02/16/a3); the 13th edition drew 1.2 million+ visitors (https://www.sharjahtourism.ae/news/12-day-sharjah-light-festival-concludes-with-an-impressive-turnout-of-over-1-2-million-visitors/). SIBF 45th: 4 to 15 November 2026, Oman guest of honour (https://www.gulftoday.ae/news/2026/07/07/45th-sharjah-international-book-fair-set-for-november-4); the 44th drew 1,400,730 visitors and 2,350 exhibitors from 118 countries (https://gulfnews.com/uae/people/sharjah-book-fair-wraps-up-with-over-14-million-visitors-from-206-countries-1.500349566). SITTF 13th: Wednesday 28 October 2026, Al Jawaher Centre; the site still shows the 12th edition theme, so confirm (https://shf.sharjahtourism.ae/). The 2025 hackathon winner was "Sharjah Quest", a gamified digital-stamp itinerary app (https://sharjah24.ae/en/Articles/2025/11/06/Innovation-Hackathon-reimagines-tourism-experience-at-AUS). Summer Promotions 2026 ran 114 days and generated Dh850 million (https://gulfnews.com/business/economy/sharjah-summer-promotions-generate-dh850-million-in-economic-returns-1.500677836).

## (e) Designations

Capital of Arab Culture 1998, Islamic Culture 2014, Arab Tourism 2015 (https://sdc.gov.ae/En/NewsDetails/304/6); WHO Healthy City, first in the region, 30 September 2015 (https://www.khaleejtimes.com/uae/who-declares-sharjah-as-regions-first-healthy-city); UNICEF Child Friendly City, first under 2018 criteria (https://www.childfriendlycities.org/sharjah-united-arab-emirates); World Book Capital 23 April 2019 to 22 April 2020 (https://www.ifla.org/?p=110324); Creative City of Crafts and Folk Art 2019 (https://gulfnews.com/opinion/op-eds/sharjah-is-a-unesco-designated-creative-city-of-culture-1.1572617968810); UNESCO Learning City September 2022 (https://www.wam.ae/en/article/hszrfhu3-unesco-grants-sharjah-membership-global-network); Faya World Heritage 2025.

## (f) Pain points

Heat and seasonality: August average high about 42°C (https://www.dubai-online.com/essential/sharjah-weather/); a University of Sharjah study (Al-Adab Journal, September 2024) found "weakness of tourism activity during the summer period" and recommended year-round planning (https://doi.org/10.31973/xbst4j72); flagship events cluster November to February. Short stays: two nights average (Cavendish). Crowding: Khorfakkan entrances and Corniche jam on Eid and weekends (https://gulftoday.ae/News/2023/04/22/Residents-make-most-of-Eid-holidays-with-outings-and-musical-shows-in-UAE); 90% of Sharjah commuters report jams on the Dubai road (https://gulfnews.com/uae/90-of-dubai-sharjah-commuters-hit-by-traffic-jams-new-study-finds-1.500181486). Wayfinding: the only tourist bus is Shurooq's City Sightseeing with 13 stops (https://www.thenationalnews.com/uae/sharjah-brings-in-tour-buses-1.405393); no Sharjah visitor wayfinding or satisfaction survey was found. Language: Russia 21% and China fastest growing; SCTDA's own chatbot shipped in Russian and Chinese. Dry emirate: alcohol prohibited including hotels (https://www.frommers.com/destinations/sharjah/planning-a-trip/).

candidates.name: Quiet Hours Dispersal Routing
candidates.one_liner: A routing layer that scores every stop by hour-of-day busyness and nudges visitors away from peak slots at Sharjah City landmarks toward under-visited East Coast and Central Region sites, showing the time cost of each swap in one plain sentence.
candidates.sustainability_link: Addresses overtourism directly. SCTDA structures its destination site and its Sustainability Map around three regions (Sharjah City, Central Region, East Coast), and this feature spreads load across them, lifting demand at under-visited sites that Visit Sharjah itself describes as a 'rare gem' (Shees Village) or 'one of the most pristine natural reserves in the Middle East' (Wadi Al Helo), alongside Nahwa Enclave and Al Rafisah Dam. Peak load is a real SCTDA problem: the 2024 Sharjah Light Festival drew over 1.2 million visitors in 12 days.
candidates.demo_in_two_days: Build a JSON of 20 to 25 sites with curated hourly busyness curves (0 to 100) and region tags copied from Visit Sharjah and the 15 places on the Sustain Sharjah Sustainability Map. Implement one scoring function: busyness at the planned hour plus a travel-time penalty. A Leaflet or MapLibre map recolors pins as a time slider moves; the itinerary panel offers one-click swaps with a generated sentence such as 'Swapping Al Noor Island at 14:00 for Kalba Corniche Park at 16:30 adds 40 minutes and avoids the daily peak.' Busyness curves are curated and labeled illustrative; the data structure accepts a real feed later. About three hours for two people.
candidates.differentiation: Last year's winner rewarded visitors with points and badges for reaching places; this changes where and when they go with no reward mechanic and shows the destination-side benefit. SCTDA's Sustainability Map lists eco-friendly spots but has no routing, crowding, or time dimension, so this fills a gap in an existing SCTDA product rather than duplicating it.
candidates.risk: Judges will ask for real crowd data; the honest answer is curated curves with an architecture ready for turnstile, telecom, or popular-times style feeds. It can look like a duplicate of the team's core route planner unless the pitch frames it as the destination-side policy layer sitting on top of the visitor-side planner, with the trade-off made visible.

candidates.name: Cool Windows Heat-Aware Scheduler
candidates.one_liner: Reorders the day's stops around live temperature, apparent temperature, and UV so exposed sites fall in cool windows and indoor museums fill the midday peak, with a shoulder-season suggestion when the whole day is too hot.
candidates.sustainability_link: Keeps tourism viable year-round in a hot climate, which is the economic leg of sustainability, and protects visitor health. It supports SCTDA's current summer campaign ('Exceptional Offers for an Unforgettable Summer' on visitsharjah.com) by making summer itineraries safe, and it reduces the idling of air-conditioned vehicles used as cooling shelters during badly timed outdoor stops.
candidates.demo_in_two_days: Open-Meteo returns Sharjah hourly data with no API key. A live call today (10 October 2026) gave 33.6 C at 09:00, 38.3 C at 12:00, 37.3 C at 15:00, an apparent temperature peak of 40.8 C at 13:00, and a UV index of 7.15. Tag each site indoor, shaded, or exposed; compute a comfort score per hour; sort the itinerary and draw a timeline with red, amber, and green windows. One fetch, one sort, one timeline component. Under two hours.
candidates.differentiation: No treasure hunt mechanics, and no regional tourism app exposes heat windows as a planning primitive. It is live data in the demo, which judges rarely see at hackathons, and it is specific to the Gulf rather than a port of a European overtourism tool.
candidates.risk: The sustainability link is indirect and must be stated in one sentence or judges will file it under convenience. On an October demo day the contrast is modest, so include a July scenario toggle using a stored Open-Meteo sample so the reordering is visible.

candidates.name: Conservation Mode in Protected Areas
candidates.one_liner: When a route enters an EPAA protected area or conservation center, the guide switches to a conservation mode: trail-only navigation, habitat and species context, rules on litter, fires, drones, and wildlife distance, and a leave-no-trace check-out.
candidates.sustainability_link: Direct environmental protection at the sites most at risk from visitor growth. Grounded in the Environment and Protected Areas Authority's protected areas (Alqurm, Wasit Nature Reserve, Lehhfaiiah, Wadil helo, Meleiha), its learning centers (Wasit Wetland Centre, Al Hefaiyah Mountain Conservation Centre, Kalba Bird of Prey Centre), and its named 'Mountain Areas Preservation Campaign' and 'Wilderness Areas Goer Campaign'. Al Qurm protects over 500 hectares of mangroves according to Sustain Sharjah.
candidates.demo_in_two_days: Draw approximate polygons for four or five protected areas as GeoJSON, detect entry from a simulated GPS position on the map, swap the UI theme and content, and show a rules card plus a species card per area drawn from EPAA public pages. A check-out screen records a self-declared leave-no-trace confirmation. No AR required; it can also drive the AR overlay if that module lands. About three hours.
candidates.differentiation: Behavior change through context rather than points. It gives the AR guide a reason to exist in nature sites, where last year's treasure hunt would be actively harmful, and it is the only candidate that makes the app protective of the environment rather than merely lower-impact.
candidates.risk: Polygons are approximate and must be labeled so. EPAA, not SCTDA, owns the areas, so the pitch should name both authorities. A self-declared leave-no-trace confirmation is weak evidence; present it as the hook for future ranger validation.

candidates.name: Local Spend Router
candidates.one_liner: Routes food, craft, guide, and transfer spend to Sharjah-owned small businesses (souq artisans, Al Dhaid farm produce, Kalba and Khorfakkan family operators) and shows the share of the itinerary budget that stays in the local economy.
candidates.sustainability_link: Community economic sustainability: tourism income retained by residents rather than chains. Heart of Sharjah states that 'artisans still practice age-old trades' in the restored district around Souq Al Shanasiyah; Visit Sharjah presents Al Dhaid as a farming town; the East Coast has small dive and boat operators (Khorfakkan lists seven dive sites on Sustain Sharjah).
candidates.demo_in_two_days: A curated list of 30 to 40 businesses with a local-ownership flag and category, a retention percentage computed from the itinerary's planned spend categories, and swap suggestions such as 'replace mall lunch with Souq Al Shanasiyah'. Data from public listings with unverified entries marked. No booking integration. About two hours.
candidates.differentiation: Shifts the value question from the visitor's rewards to the resident's income, which is what a tourism authority answers to. Last year's hunt sent people to places; this sends money to people.
candidates.risk: Ownership data is hard to verify in hours and a wrong 'local' label on a chain would be embarrassing in front of SCTDA. The Irthi Contemporary Crafts Council site was under construction when checked, so do not cite its Bidwa artisans without another source. Spend categories are self-reported, so the percentage is an estimate.

candidates.name: Visitor Load Forecast Panel for SCTDA
candidates.one_liner: An authority-facing view that aggregates anonymized itinerary intent into an hourly load forecast per site and counts how many visits the dispersal and heat nudges moved, functioning as a lightweight digital twin of visitor flow.
candidates.sustainability_link: Gives SCTDA the measurement layer that sustainable destination management requires. When SCTDA launched its Sustainable Tourism AI Assistant in October 2024 it cited the UN World Tourism Organisation initiative 'Towards a Statistical Framework for Measuring Sustainability'; a per-site load forecast is a concrete input to that framework. Sharjah received about 1.6 million hotel guests in 2024, up 11%, so growth management is a live concern.
candidates.demo_in_two_days: Generate a few hundred synthetic itineraries at page load, aggregate into a site-by-hour heat map, a forecast-versus-capacity line chart, and a 'visits redirected' counter. Chart.js or Recharts, no backend. Label synthetic clearly on screen. About two hours once candidate 1 exists.
candidates.differentiation: Most hackathon tourism apps stop at the visitor. This gives the ecosystem partner in the room its own screen and turns the consumer app into a data asset for policy. It also upgrades the team's existing 'anonymized visitor analytics' bullet into something visible.
candidates.risk: Entirely synthetic data can read as a slide rather than a product. Privacy questions about intent aggregation need an answer (on-device aggregation, minimum group sizes). It depends on candidate 1 or 2 existing to have anything to forecast.

candidates.name: Sustain Sharjah Journey Connector
candidates.one_liner: The guide prefers and labels hotels and destinations that have completed levels of SCTDA's Sustain Sharjah Sustainability Journey, and gives destinations a visitor-side evidence export (dispersal, off-peak share, local spend) for their Sustain Sharjah Awards application.
candidates.sustainability_link: Plugs into SCTDA's own certification ladder. The Sustain Sharjah Awards 2026 require Level 1 (Foundation) with at least 80 points, or Level 2 (Explorer) for returning participants, and recipients are recognized at the Sharjah International Travel and Tourism Forum on 28 October 2026. The hackathon winner presents at SITTF 2026, so the feature and the stage are the same event.
candidates.demo_in_two_days: A curated list of the 15 Sustainability Map places plus the accommodation listings (The Chedi Al Bait, Kingfisher Retreat, Moon Retreat, Al Badayer Retreat), each with an illustrative journey-level badge; a ranking boost in recommendations; a one-page HTML 'evidence pack' generated from the demo analytics. About two hours.
candidates.differentiation: Turns the app into a distribution channel for an existing SCTDA program rather than a parallel scheme. Rewards for visitors (last year) become evidence for businesses (this year).
candidates.risk: Journey completion data is private, so every badge in the demo is illustrative and must be labeled. The feature is a connector rather than a capability, so it is weak alone; it is strongest as the pitch frame wrapped around candidates 1, 2, or 3.

candidates.name: Itinerary Carbon and Water Ledger
candidates.one_liner: A running footprint for the itinerary (transport carbon per leg, water intensity per overnight) with one-tap greener swaps such as a shared transfer, a single East Coast base instead of daily round trips, or a Sustain Sharjah listed stay.
candidates.sustainability_link: Makes the environmental cost of each choice visible at decision time. It extends SCTDA's own Tourist Carbon calculator on sustainsharjah.com, which is account-gated and trip-level, into an open, leg-by-leg view inside the guide, and adds water, which matters more than carbon in the Gulf.
candidates.demo_in_two_days: Static emission factors per mode (car, taxi, bus, walk) and a per-night water band per accommodation type in a JSON file with the source named on screen; totals update as the itinerary changes; a swap panel shows the delta in kg CO2 and liters. Credit the factor table in the AI Usage Disclosure and on the slide. About two hours.
candidates.differentiation: The pitch must stress what is new relative to SCTDA's calculator: itinerary-level, live while planning, and paired with water. Nothing gamified; the number itself is the feedback.
candidates.risk: Highest risk of 'SCTDA already has this'. Factor accuracy will be challenged by the data mentors (Alaa Elkouni, Rohan Mitra), so every factor needs a cited source. Per-hotel water figures do not exist publicly, so bands must be clearly labeled as estimates.

candidates.name: Round-Up for Restoration
candidates.one_liner: At heritage stops the guide shows the site's conservation status and offers a micro-contribution (a round-up on a ticket or a 5 AED tap) toward a named restoration item, with a public ledger of what visitors funded.
candidates.sustainability_link: Channels tourism revenue directly into cultural heritage conservation, the heritage pillar of sustainable tourism. Anchors to Heart of Sharjah, where Souq Al Shanasiyah, The Chedi Al Bait, and restored homes show what restoration produces, and to forts on the East Coast and in the Central Region (Dibba Al-Hisn Fort, Khor Kalba Fort, Al Dhaid Fort).
candidates.demo_in_two_days: A mock payment sheet (no real transaction), a ledger view with three or four restoration items and progress bars, and a before-and-after slider reusing the planned time-travel 3D or AR assets. Curated content per site; contribution records stored locally. About two hours.
candidates.differentiation: Replaces reward-seeking with giving; the visitor leaves something at the site rather than collecting points from it. Few guide apps tie micro-donations to itemized, visible conservation outcomes.
candidates.risk: Who receives funds and under what authority is a governance question the team cannot answer; present it as a model that Sharjah Museums Authority or Shurooq would operate. Payments cannot be real in the demo. Judges may view donation features as low technical contribution.

candidates.name: Slow Trail: Three Days on the East Coast
candidates.one_liner: Multi-day slow-tourism trails that keep visitors at one base (Khorfakkan, Kalba, or Dibba Al Hisn) for two or three nights, replacing daily round trips from Sharjah City with walking, kayaking, and short hops.
candidates.sustainability_link: Longer stays with fewer vehicle kilometers, more spend in East Coast towns, and lower pressure on city sites. Uses stays and trails already promoted on Sustain Sharjah (Kingfisher Retreat, Moon Retreat, Wadi Shees Nature Trail, Mleiha Fossil Rock Hiking Trail) and East Coast sites from Visit Sharjah (Kalba Corniche Park, Al Hefaiyah Mountain Conservation Centre, Shees Village, Wadi Al Helo).
candidates.demo_in_two_days: Three curated trail templates as JSON, a day-by-day view with distance and transport mode per leg, and a comparison card against the equivalent city-based day trips (kilometers, hours in a car, nights in the region). Static content on the planner's existing map. About two hours.
candidates.differentiation: Changes the shape of the trip rather than adding a game. The comparison card against day trips is the novel element; most itinerary tools optimize within a day, not across the structure of the trip.
candidates.risk: Reads as curated content more than technology, so technical contribution scores may suffer. Distances must be checked against a routing API or map, not guessed.

candidates.name: Calm Route Profile (low-sensory and step-free)
candidates.one_liner: A route profile for autistic, elderly, and mobility-limited visitors that prefers shaded, quiet, step-free paths, schedules rest and prayer stops, and warns about crowd and noise peaks.
candidates.sustainability_link: Social sustainability and inclusion: tourism that all visitors and residents can take part in, and that spreads visitors into quieter hours by design. Reuses the busyness data from candidate 1 and the shade and heat data from candidate 2.
candidates.demo_in_two_days: A toggle that changes route weights, a filtered site list with icons for shade, seating, step-free access, and quiet hours, and one sample route shown before and after. Accessibility attributes curated for about 15 sites. Under two hours.
candidates.differentiation: A profile, not a game. Few regional tourism apps offer a sensory profile rather than a generic accessibility page.
candidates.risk: Overlaps the team's existing accessibility bullet (audio descriptions, subtitles, simplified navigation), so it may not read as a replacement feature. Accessibility attributes are unverified and errors harm real users; label them community-reported.

result.recommendation: Pick candidate 1, Quiet Hours Dispersal Routing. It is the only candidate that is at once SCTDA's stated priority (the authority organizes its destination site and Sustainability Map around Sharjah City, the Central Region, and the East Coast), unambiguous as sustainability (moving load off peaks and toward under-visited sites), buildable this afternoon with curated hourly busyness curves, and productive of the impact number judges will ask for (share of visits moved off-peak or out of the city). It reuses the planned route planner and feeds the authority analytics feature for free. If time remains on Day 2, add candidate 2's heat windows as a second signal in the same scoring function. No points or badges; the incentive is a quieter, cooler visit.

result.type_display: IBM Plex Sans Condensed, SemiBold 600, for HUD labels, callout headings, mode tabs, and deck headings; Arabic companion IBM Plex Sans Arabic SemiBold 600 (no condensed cut exists, so Arabic labels are given 20 percent more panel width). Both confirmed on Google Fonts.
result.type_body: IBM Plex Sans Regular 400 and Medium 500 for prose and the guide chat, 15 to 16px, line length capped at 60ch inside panels; IBM Plex Mono Regular with tabular figures for every readout (meters, minutes, crowd index, grams CO2, shade fraction); IBM Plex Sans Arabic Regular 400 for Arabic prose, Eastern Arabic digits optional per locale. One superfamily, three cuts, width and mono as the contrast axes.
result.layout: The live camera is the home screen and the only full-bleed surface. Three layers sit on it. Layer one is the feed, untouched. Layer two is the callout system: a recognized or heading-matched landmark gets four 1px corner ticks (a reticle, never a closed box), a hairline leader line, and one glass panel with three fixed rows: name and year, one fact, and a sustainability strip (shade now, crowd now, grams CO2 to walk there). Lens callouts draw the leader line with stroke-dashoffset over 300ms, then the label fades in 160ms later; one callout animates at a time. The guide sheet slides up with transform over 320ms and its list items stagger 60ms. The capacity meter fills once with a 480ms ease-out on first view. Under prefers-reduced-motion: 120ms crossfades, static water, meter rendered at its final state.
result.imagery: Field-guide plates, not photography-led. Each site and species gets a flat two-tone vector plate (silt fill, mangrove-ink line at one consistent weight, one kingfisher or flamingo spot color) in the manner of a naturalist's identification plate with a numbered caption. Demo species: Avicennia marina, Arabian collared kingfisher, greater flamingo, mudskipper, ghost crab; heritage set: Kalba fort, Wasit bird hides, a Heart of Sharjah wind tower. Photography appears only inside a site plate as a muted-toned, full-width image with a 1px silt border and a captioned credit; no hero photo, no skyline drone shot, no generated people. For the hackathon, plates come from CC-licensed illustrations on Wikimedia Commons or the Biodiversity Heritage Library, recolored to the palette and credited on the credits page and in the AI Usage Disclosure, or from one consistent generated plate style if time allows.
result.hero_prompt: Flat field-guide illustration plate of Khor Kalba mangroves at low tide: gray mangrove trees with pencil roots in silt-green water, an Arabian collared kingfisher on a branch, a pale coral-stone watchtower far behind, overcast Gulf light, muted sage, silt gray, kingfisher teal, dusty rose, two-tone vector shapes, even line weight, no text, no people.
result.why_sharjah: Khor Kalba's gray mangroves shelter the Arabian collared kingfisher, found nowhere else; Wasit Wetland Centre's reed beds, bird hides, and flamingos (Aga Khan Award 2019); sabkha flats and creek silt; coral-stone and gypsum walls of the Heart of Sharjah; the hazy overcast Gulf light that flattens shadows and favors soft greens over hard contrast.
result.why_sustainable: Habitats and species are first-class map objects beside monuments. Every site carries a tide-gauge capacity meter and a quiet-hours layer that steers visitors from crowded hides to open ones. Two-tone plates and no video backgrounds keep pages light. Conservation data is credited to EPAA sources, visible rather than decorative.

result.type_display: EB Garamond (weights 400 and 500) at 40 to 48px on phone and a 72px cap on desktop, letter-spacing 0 to -0.01em, with Amiri as the Arabic companion for headings and place names. Amiri is a revival of the Bulaq Press naskh used in early Arabic book printing, which ties the display face directly to the World Book Capital theme. Both are on Google Fonts.
result.type_body: IBM Plex Sans 17/26 for body copy and UI controls, IBM Plex Sans Arabic for Arabic body text (the two are drawn to share metrics), and IBM Plex Mono 12px uppercase reserved for plate captions and ledger figures only. Marginal notes are set in EB Garamond 14/20. Three families, each with one job; Inter is not used anywhere. Separate line-height tokens for Arabic and Latin runs.
result.layout: Phone first on a 4-column grid, 8px baseline, 16px gutters; the desktop judging demo at 1200px becomes a two-page spread on 12 columns with a 72ch measure. The app is one book. Navigation is a running head at the top: Index (map), Plate (AR view), Colophon (the day's ledger), set as three serif words over a hairline rule with the active word in rubric red; there is no icon tab bar. The AR camera view is the plate: it fills the top 60 percent of the leaf inside a hairline frame with a mono caption (Plate 7. Al Hisn Fort, east wall, coral stone). The guide chat is not a separate screen. Following the matn-and-hashiya convention of Arabic manuscripts, where commentary sits in the margin beside the main text, the guide's replies appear as numbered marginal notes beside the plate (right margin in English, mirrored to the left in Arabic). Tapping a red numeral on a landmark in the camera opens its note, and the question field sits at the foot of the margin where a reader would write a gloss. The map is the index: a single-color line map in lapis on the same page tone, routes as hairlines, sites listed beneath as index entries with leaf numbers, so a visitor reads the day as a table of contents. Density is high by app standards: text is the interface, blocks are separated by rules and whitespace, and cards are not used.
result.motion: Marginal note numerals stamp in (scale 1.06 to 1, 120ms, ease-out-expo) when the camera recognizes a landmark, and a hairline leader draws from the landmark to its note with a clip-path reveal over 240ms. Guide replies are set a line at a time, like a typesetter filling a column (opacity per line, 80ms stagger), never a per-character typewriter. Leaves slide horizontally between Index, Plate, and Colophon (translateX 24px to 0 with opacity, 280ms, ease-out-quint). No page curl, no parallax, no bounce. Reduced motion replaces all of it with 150ms crossfades.
result.imagery: Documentary photography of real Sharjah places, taken by the team during the event after 16:30 when the coral stone warms and shadows lengthen; full color printed flat, with no vignette, sepia, or filter. Photographs appear only as plates: hairline frame, mono caption with plate number, place, material, and year. Historical views use published archive photographs with credit lines, never AI reconstructions. No illustration, no arabesque pattern, no geometric wallpaper; the Arabic type itself is the ornament.
result.hero_prompt: Open hardbound folio resting on a coral-stone ledge in Heart of Sharjah, late afternoon light, typeset pages with red rubric headings and Arabic naskh marginal notes, a phone lying on the page showing the same layout as an AR overlay on Al Hisn Fort wall, documentary photography, flat natural color, no gradients, no glow, shallow depth of field.
result.why_sharjah: Sharjah was UNESCO World Book Capital 2019 and hosts the Sharjah International Book Fair and House of Wisdom library. The heritage area holds the Sharjah Calligraphy Museum and Al Hisn Fort's coral-stone walls. Amiri revives the Bulaq Press naskh of early Arabic printing. Rubric red and lapis come from manuscript illumination, not from a trend palette.
result.why_sustainable: The margin keeps a ledger: meters walked, bus rides, dirhams spent with souq craftsmen, water refills. The day closes with a colophon page that totals it. AR annotates existing walls instead of rendering replacements, and the page is text and hairlines, so it loads on weak signal with low energy.

references.what: DESIGN.md with black ink on #F5F1E8, 0px radius, no shadows or gradients, hierarchy from weight and spacing in three to four sizes, mono reserved for metadata. Taken for the rule that type alone carries hierarchy.

result.slop_guardrails: No parchment or paper-grain textures (no feTurbulence), no sepia, no burnt or torn edges, no page curl. No warm cream drift: the page stays at #EFEFED with chroma near zero. No AI-generated Arabic calligraphy; every Arabic string is live text in Amiri or IBM Plex Sans Arabic, shaped and mirrored for RTL. No arabesque or geometric wallpaper, no gold on cream, no drop cap on every paragraph. The note numerals are the only numbered system and each must index a real note; no 01/02/03 section eyebrows. No HDR glow, no drone shots with purple skies, no 3D renders, no AI-generated skylines. Marketing posters take a two-color treatment (navy plus one accent) over the photo with the headline cut across it; inside the app the photo stays full color under solid type. Arabic companion: Readex Pro 700 (Google Fonts, arabic subset confirmed in google/fonts METADATA), set 10 percent larger than the Latin to match x-height and right-aligned on the same plate.

Three families in total (Overpass, Atkinson Hyperlegible, Readex Pro), no Inter, no fourth family.
result.layout: Mobile-first 4-column grid, 16px gutters, 8px baseline, organized as three fixed horizontal zones like a station. Zone 1 is a 64px sign header plate in the surface color carrying the current place name in Latin and Arabic, a route number plate, and a three-cell crowd gauge. Zone 2 is the stage, which shows either the live AR camera or the map, switched by one two-cell toggle, never both at once. Zone 3 is a bottom platform bar with three pictogram tabs: Look (AR), Map, Ask (guide). Route bands are full-width horizontal strips 12px tall in green, blue, or amber stacked under the header like transit line indicators, and the same bands draw as 6px lines on a desaturated gray basemap. The guide chat is not a floating bubble layer: it slides up as a stacked sign plate over the lower 45 percent of the stage; each answer is a dark plate with white text, suggested questions are route-colored chips (ink text on amber, white on green and blue), and tapping a place name inside an answer drops the plate and pins that place on the map or anchors it in the AR view. AR overlays are anchored sign plates with a band on their top edge and flat chevrons drawn on the ground plane like road markings. The desktop pitch view keeps the same three zones with the map at 60 percent width and the plates in a 40 percent column; no cards anywhere.
result.motion: Signage moves like signage. Plates enter with an 8px translateY over 180ms ease-out-quart, no bounce, no elastic. A chosen route band draws along its path with stroke-dashoffset over 400ms. The crowd gauge fills cell by cell at 90ms steps like an LED board. The Latin and Arabic toggle uses a 240ms vertical clip-path wipe, a nod to the split-flap board, with plate height fixed so nothing reflows. AR chevrons step through three opacity states at 600ms intervals instead of glowing. Under prefers-reduced-motion every one of these becomes a 120ms crossfade.
result.imagery: Documentary photography of Sharjah in daylight, full-bleed and uncropped, no teal-orange grading, no filters: coral-stone walls in the Heart of Sharjah, Blue Souk tiles, Kalba mangroves, Mleiha rock, Khor Fakkan's Hajar slopes. Photos never sit under text; captions live on plates beside them. Pictograms are a bespoke set of eight drawn on a 24px grid at 2.5px stroke in the AIGA/DOT tradition: walk, abra, bus, shade, water refill, mangrove, fort, souk. Material Symbols, credited in the AI and open-source disclosure, fill any gap. No 3D renders, no isometric illustration, no AI sparkle glyphs.
result.hero_prompt: Documentary photograph, Sharjah Corniche, 16:00 hard sunlight. Foreground: a tall matte black wayfinding totem with oversized white Latin and Arabic place names, three horizontal bands in mangrove green, souk blue, and desert amber, and white pictograms of a walking figure, an abra boat, and a mangrove. Blue Souk tiles and the creek behind. Flat colors, no glow, no gradients.
result.why_sharjah: The three route bands take their colors from places on the routes themselves: Blue Souk tile blue, Kalba mangrove green, and Mleiha's amber rock. The neutral board recalls the whitewashed courtyards of the Sharjah Art Foundation and the coral-stone of the Heart of Sharjah. Bilingual plates follow the road and museum signs visitors already read along the Corniche.
result.why_sustainable: Every route band is a footprint label: green for walking and shaded paths, blue for creek water transport, amber for motorized or peak-heat legs. Crowd gauges borrow the parking-sign idiom to disperse visitors toward Mleiha, Kalba, and Khor Fakkan. Flat print-grade graphics run on low-end phones without heavy rendering.

result.slop_guardrails: Never a gradient of any kind, never glass or blur over the camera, never purple or blue-purple, never a cream or sand body. Bands are full-width horizontal strips only, never a left-border stripe on a card. Corner radius 0 to 4px on plates; pills only on 24px chips. No emoji pictograms, no sparkle or AI glyph, no chat-bubble tails, no shadow wider than 8px. No uppercase body copy, no tracked eyebrow kickers, no 01/02/03 scaffolding outside the route index. No decorative Arabic calligraphy as texture, no fake highway exit jokes, no stock photos of Dubai standing in for Sharjah.
result.risks: Judges may read the sternness as a transport utility rather than a tourism product, so the photography has to carry the warmth in the deck.
